title: Algebra and Functions: From Patterns to Mappings
description: A connected course from concrete number patterns through variables, sets, equations, function composition and inverse mappings.

modules.description: Develop algebraic reasoning through proof, representation and computation.

modules.description: Develop algebraic reasoning through proof, representation and computation.

objectives.title: Whole-number structure and additive patterns
objectives.description: Whole numbers can be explored through order, parity, repeated addition, and additive patterns; conjectures about such patterns must be stated with an explicit domain.

objectives.title: Variables and algebraic expressions
objectives.description: A variable can represent a changing or unknown quantity, allowing a relationship observed in concrete cases to be expressed as a general rule.

objectives.title: Sets, relations and functions
objectives.description: Sets, relations and functions provide a common language for defining mathematical objects, mappings and domains.

objectives.title: Equations and inequalities
objectives.description: Equations and inequalities express constraints on unknown quantities; valid transformations preserve the solution set under stated conditions.

objectives.title: Functions, composition and inverse mappings
objectives.description: Functions map each element of a declared domain to exactly one codomain element; composition and inverses obey domain and range constraints.

lessons.title: Discover counting patterns
lessons.body: Begin with concrete groups and growing arrangements. Compare 1, 3, 5, 7, 9; notice the constant difference before writing a general rule.

stages.prompt: Arrange objects in a row, then add one more pair. What changes?
Compare 1, 3, 5, 7, and 9. Describe the change from one term to the next.
Draw the growing groups and identify what remains unchanged.
Explain why each new odd number is two more than the previous one.
Only after explaining the pattern, state the nth odd number as 2n − 1.

exercise.objective: Recognize additive structure and express a pattern in general form.
exercise.prompt: Find the 10th term of 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, ... State a rule for the nth odd number and verify it at three positions.
hints: Start at 1 and add 2 for every step after the first.

rubric.description: Identifies the constant difference of two.
States a correct nth-term rule.
Checks at least three positions.

exercise.transfer_prompt: Start at 4 and add 3 each time. Give the nth-term rule and compare it with the odd-number rule.

lessons.title: Model a changing quantity
lessons.body: A jar begins with four coins and receives three more coins each minute. Build a table and describe the relationship before using a variable.

stages.prompt: Imagine a jar receiving one or more coins at a constant rate.
Record the amount after zero, one, two, three, and four minutes.
Plot elapsed time against the number of coins.
Explain the starting amount and the repeated increase.
Represent the relationship as 4 + 3m, defining m.

exercise.objective: Interpret a variable as a name for a changing or unknown quantity.
exercise.prompt: A jar starts with 4 coins and receives 3 more coins each minute. Make a table for the first five minutes and write a rule for the number of coins after m minutes.
hints: Separate the starting amount from the repeated increase.
The amount added is the same each minute.
A letter can stand for any allowed number of minutes.

rubric.description: Builds an accurate table.
Explains the starting amount and repeated increase.
Writes and interprets 4 + 3m.

exercise.transfer_prompt: Change the jar so it starts with 7 coins and receives 2 coins per minute. Write and explain the new rule.

lessons.title: Sets, relations and functions
lessons.body: Use collections of objects to distinguish membership, subset, relation and function. A function is a special relation: each input in its declared domain has exactly one output in its codomain.
lessons.historical_context: Set language became a shared foundation for modern mathematics. The lesson focuses on the practical distinction between a general relation and a single-valued mapping.

stages.prompt: Make two groups of cards: students and books. Draw arrows from each student to the books they borrowed.
Can one student point to two books? Can one student point to no book? What changes if the arrows represent a function assigning each student exactly one locker?
Draw a mapping diagram with a domain on the left and codomain on the right. Compare a many-to-one function with a relation that gives one input two outputs.
Define domain, codomain, image, relation and function in your own words. Give one example that is a relation but not a function.
Represent a function f from A to B and state the condition that each element of A has exactly one image in B.

exercise.objective: Classify relations and explain when a relation is a function.
exercise.prompt: Let A = {a,b,c} and B = {1,2,3}. Consider R = {(a,1),(b,2),(c,2)} and S = {(a,1),(a,2),(b,3)}. Decide whether each is a function from A to B. Explain using the domain rule, then give one relation that is not a function because an input has no output.
hints: Check every element of A, not only the elements that appear in the ordered pairs.
A function cannot assign two different outputs to the same input.
A relation can be incomplete or multi-valued; those are not functions from the full declared domain.

rubric.description: States the one-output rule for every domain element.
Correctly classifies R and S from their ordered pairs.
Constructs a valid non-function example and explains why it fails.

exercise.transfer_prompt: Model a program that maps each user ID to a single account record. Give an example of data that violates the function contract.

lessons.title: Equations and inequalities as constraints
lessons.body: An equation describes values that make two expressions equal. An inequality describes an ordered constraint. Valid transformations preserve the solution set, but dividing by zero or multiplying an inequality by a negative number requires special care.
lessons.historical_context: Algebra developed as a systematic language for unknown quantities and transformations. The key idea here is not symbol manipulation alone: each step must preserve the set of valid solutions.

stages.prompt: Imagine a balanced scale. If both sides have the same amount added, does the balance change? What if one side is divided by zero?
Try several values in 2x + 3 = 11. Notice which value makes both sides equal and how the balance changes under the same operation on each side.
Place x values on a number line. Show the solution set of x > 2 and compare it with the single solution of x = 2.
Explain the difference between an equation and an inequality. Describe why multiplying an inequality by a negative number reverses its direction.
Solve 3x + 5 = 20 and -2x + 4 ≤ 10. State the solution set and justify each transformation.

exercise.objective: Solve equations and inequalities while preserving their solution sets.
exercise.prompt: Solve 3x + 5 = 20 and -2x + 4 ≤ 10. For each step, name the operation and explain why it preserves equivalence. Verify one solution and one non-solution for the inequality.
hints: Undo addition or subtraction before undoing multiplication.
When dividing an inequality by a negative number, reverse the inequality symbol.
Substitute a proposed solution into the original statement, not only the transformed one.

rubric.description: Explains equations and inequalities as solution-set constraints.
Performs valid transformations and obtains correct solutions.
Represents the inequality solution set on a number line or interval.
Checks a solution and a non-solution in the original inequality.

exercise.transfer_prompt: A sensor must stay between 18 and 24 units inclusive. Express the constraint as an inequality and explain how a calibration offset changes the allowed raw readings.

lessons.title: Functions, composition and inverse mappings
lessons.body: A function is a mapping from a declared domain to a codomain in which every input has exactly one output. Composition chains mappings; an inverse reverses a mapping only when the relevant one-to-one and onto conditions hold, or when the domain is restricted appropriately.
lessons.historical_context: Coordinate geometry and modern function notation helped unify algebraic rules with geometric and computational representations. A function is more than a formula: its domain and codomain are part of the object.

stages.prompt: Use an input-output machine: put in a number, double it, then add one. Record several inputs and outputs.
Compare two machines. Does each input always produce exactly one output? Can two different inputs produce the same output and still form a function?
Build a table and graph for f(x) = 2x + 1. Mark the input domain and output values.
Explain domain, codomain, image, composition, injective and inverse. Give an example where an inverse function does not exist on the original domain.
Let f(x)=2x+1 and g(x)=x². Compare (g∘f)(2) with (f∘g)(2). Find the inverse of f and state its domain and codomain.

exercise.objective: Translate functions between rules and mappings, compose them, and identify inverse conditions.
exercise.prompt: Let f(x)=2x+1 and g(x)=x² over the real numbers. Compute (g∘f)(2) and (f∘g)(2). Find f⁻¹ and verify both inverse compositions. Explain why g has no inverse function over all real numbers without restricting its domain.
hints: Composition order matters: (g∘f)(x) means apply f first, then g.
For f(x)=2x+1, undo the addition before undoing multiplication.
The square function maps x and -x to the same output, so it is not injective over all real numbers.

rubric.description: Explains function contracts and inverse conditions.
Correctly expresses composition as ordered mapping operations.
Computes compositions and inverse correctly.
Identifies why domain restriction is needed for the square function.

exercise.transfer_prompt: Model a Celsius-to-Fahrenheit conversion and its inverse. State the domain and codomain and explain whether the conversion is one-to-one.
